planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, protecting from hot late-afternoon sun; sawtooth stewartia dislikes root disturbance and transplants and establishes slowly like its relatives.

directions: Native to the mountains of Honshu, Shikoku, and Kyushu in Japan, sawtooth stewartia is distinguished from the more common Japanese stewartia by flowering later, in early to mid-summer, and by creamy-white flowers that show a distinctive red blush at the base of the petals around yellow anthers. Smooth, reddish-brown, mottled bark provides winter interest, and glossy, leathery, sharply serrated leaves, the source of its common name, turn crimson to orange-red in fall. It remains a smaller, more shrubby tree than Japanese stewartia, typically staying under 30 feet, making it well suited to smaller woodland gardens.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in neutral to acidic, moist, well-drained soil in sun to part shade in mild-winter climates; this tender, semi-evergreen stewartia needs shelter from hard freezes and drying winds and is only reliable where winters stay mild.

directions: Unlike its deciduous cousins, this Chinese and northern Vietnamese species is semi-evergreen to evergreen, with leathery, deeply veined leaves that emerge red-bronze before maturing to dark glossy green. Camellia-like white flowers with yellow centers appear in spring. Native to forests of western and southern Yunnan and northern Vietnam at high elevation, it was introduced to Western cultivation by early 20th-century plant hunters. Considerably more tender than Japanese or American stewartias, it is best suited to mild, sheltered gardens rather than typical continental climates, but rewards growers there with a rare evergreen presence in a genus best known for deciduous species.

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade, sheltered from drying winds; Hemsley's snowbell is more drought tolerant than S. obassia once established but still prefers good, moist soil.

directions: Hemsley's snowbell is a conical deciduous tree from central China, bearing large rounded leaves and pendant clusters of cup-shaped white flowers in early summer. It has earned the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit and, unlike some other early-20th-century Styrax introductions that faded from cultivation, has persisted and is grown in gardens across the British Isles and increasingly in North America. Green fruit follows the flowers, and the tree's bee-friendly blooms make it a good pollinator plant. Less common in the trade than Japanese snowbell but a worthy alternative for collectors seeking a larger-leaved, similarly refined understory tree.

common_name: Chameleon Sourwood (Uniform-Habit Selection with Multicolor Fall Foliage)

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; like the species, Chameleon resents root disturbance and requires acidic soil to thrive.

directions: Chameleon is a rare sourwood selection made at a Martha's Vineyard arboretum. It offers a more uniform, upright, conical framework than typical seedling-grown sourwoods, and its common name comes from fall foliage that shifts through a sequence of green, yellow, pink, and orange-scarlet rather than coloring all at once. Otherwise it shares the species' midsummer panicles of white, lily-of-the-valley-like flowers and requires the same strictly acidic soil.

common_name: Mt. Charm Sourwood (Early Fall Color Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Mt. Charm needs the same acidic soil and undisturbed root zone as the species.

directions: Mt. Charm is a sourwood cultivar selected for its symmetrical, conical growth habit and for being among the earliest sourwoods to color each autumn, giving gardeners a jump-start on the species' famous fiery scarlet fall display. It otherwise carries the same midsummer white flower panicles and strict requirement for acidic, well-drained soil as the straight species.

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; this rare variegated selection is otherwise as demanding of acidic soil and undisturbed roots as the species.

directions: Albomarginatum is an uncommon variegated sourwood selection with green leaves edged in white, some showing marbled white patterning, adding a lighter, variegated presence to the genus's typically solid dark-green summer foliage. It shares the species' midsummer white flower panicles and turns vividly in fall, though its variegated leaves are considered its main distinguishing feature. It remains a rare, obscure selection that has never entered wide commercial circulation, so plants are found mainly through specialty and collector nurseries.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun to part shade; Gordlinia is more vigorous and adaptable than Franklinia but still dislikes heavy, alkaline, or poorly drained soils.

directions: xGordlinia grandiflora is a bigeneric hybrid created at North Carolina State University, crossing the cold-hardy but famously finicky, extinct-in-the-wild Franklinia alatamaha with the evergreen but less cold-hardy loblolly bay, Gordonia lasianthus. The hybrid combines the vigor and greater garden adaptability of both parents, producing large, fragrant, camellia-like white flowers with prominent yellow stamens over a long season from midsummer into September, considerably longer than Franklinia's fall-only bloom window. Foliage is semi-evergreen, dropping some leaves in fall while remaining leaves show red-orange color, and the plant grows as a fast, multi-stemmed large shrub or small tree. It offers gardeners in warmer zones a way to enjoy Franklinia's flower character on a tougher, more forgiving plant.
